reasoning: The overflow is real in the code, and the scan runs by default. OpencodeScanner.swift:141-142 sums $.tokens.output and $.tokens.reasoning, :186-187 read them as Int64, and :197 adds them with a bare checked `+` that clamps each value only from below. CostEstimator.swift:44-49 and :161-164 run the scan on every cost refresh for the hard-coded provider aliases, with no config switch. No -Ounchecked or unsafeFlags turns the trap off. What fails is the source. The data comes from ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, a file in the user's home that only the user's own processes, or root, can write. The finding says so itself: its precondition is 'another tool or a prompt-injected agent running as the same user'. On this local single-user desktop app, a process that can write that file already has the same power over this app. It can kill the process, edit ~/Library/Application Support/ai-taskbar/config.toml, or delete the caches. Crashing the menu-bar app through a malformed row crosses no trust boundary and gives the attacker nothing new. No remote or lower-privileged actor controls this input: opencode itself writes token counts from real usage, and the file is opened read-only (SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY, :108). A multi-row sum that overflows makes SQLite fail the step with an integer overflow error, so :211 returns nil. That leaves only the crafted single-row case, which again needs a same-user writer. Separately, as a robustness bug (not a security vulnerability), :197 should use CostAggregator.saturatingAdd to match the other scanners.
